title: Content Cluster Launch Checklist: Final Refresh & Sitemap
description: The final launch checklist for a 28-page content cluster: content refreshes, schema verification, sitemap submission, Search Console setup, and post-launch monitoring.
ogTitle: Content Cluster Launch Checklist: Final Refresh & Sitemap
ogDescription: Final refresh, schema verification, sitemap submission, and post-launch monitoring — the closing checklist for a large content cluster.

inline: . It assumes Day 29's audit is complete and the cluster is structurally sound.

After this day, the cluster moves from "being built" to "being indexed." That is a different phase — the content is done, the internal linking is done, and now the work is monitoring indexing, watching ranking patterns, and iterating on the pages that do not perform as expected over the following 30–90 days.

Day 29 found the structural problems. Day 30 fixes the last of them, verifies the whole cluster is ready for indexing, and submits it. This is the day the cluster moves from "internally complete" to "externally live."

Day 30 is not the day to add more pages. The cluster is complete; the goal is to launch what exists.
Unless a design problem is actively breaking conversion, do not change design on launch day.
Never migrate or make major platform changes on the same day as a cluster launch. Too many variables at once.

inline: The full day takes 4–6 hours of active work, plus time for verification to propagate (sitemap submission, Search Console indexing, analytics events). Most of the active work is in steps 1 and 2; steps 3–5 are mostly configuration and confirmation.

The cluster has been built over 29 days. During that time, some things changed — internal linking was adjusted, some pages revealed gaps that needed patching, and some claims that were true on Day 1 may not be true on Day 30. This step is where you close those gaps before launch.

b: Internal links that were added during the audit.

items: If Day 29 added links from the pillar to the case study and reviews, verify those links read naturally in context — not bolted on.
If a page referred to "the case study" before the case study was published, verify the reference now points correctly.
Every page should have a "Last updated" line, and it should reflect the actual update date (which may be today's date if you refreshed the page).

b: Numbers and dates that may have shifted.

items: Pricing ranges, salary figures, or platform descriptions that were true on Day 1 may need adjustment if market data has changed during the build.
Read 3–4 random pages from different sections and confirm the voice is consistent. Inconsistency happens when a large cluster is built over weeks.

b: Pages that are already performing well.

items: If a page has been live for a week and is getting traffic, do not touch it on launch day — the risk of breaking something outweighs the marginal improvement.
If a page makes an argument, do not soften it on launch day. The argument is the reason the page exists.

b: Pages where the "refresh" would be a rewrite.

items: If a page needs a full rewrite, do it as a separate project after launch — not in a hurried patch on Day 30.
The most important page in the cluster. Verify every internal link to a cluster page works, every price range is consistent with the cost guide, every claim matches the current process.
The hub for the 7 city pages. Verify the comparison table numbers still match the individual city pages.

The trust cluster. Verify the review count in the aggregate rating matches the actual reviews, the case study numbers are consistent with the portfolio summary, and every cross-link between them works.
The commercial core. Verify pricing is consistent with the freelancer cost page and that the payment schedules match the process page.
Spot-check for internal link consistency and consistency of claims.

blocks.text: What a typical refresh looks like

inline: For most pages, the refresh is 5–15 minutes of small edits: fixing an internal link's anchor text, updating the "Last updated" date, correcting a numeric cross-reference, or smoothing a sentence where a link was added. It is not a rewrite. If a page needs more than 15 minutes of edits, it should be flagged for a post-launch update rather than fixed on launch day.
Schema has been added to each page as it was built, but schema consistency across the whole cluster has not been verified in one place. This step does that verification.

Each page should have one Article schema, one FAQPage schema (if applicable), one breadcrumb schema. Duplicate blocks confuse Google.

b: FAQ schema without visible FAQ content.

items: Google requires the schema to reflect visible content. If a page has FAQ schema but the questions are not visible, remove the schema (not add the content — that would be a different fix).
The portfolio and reviews pages can legitimately have AggregateRating (they show reviews). The pillar or cost guide should not, unless they also show reviews.

b: Review schema mismatched with visible reviews.

items: If the schema claims 5 reviews but only 3 are visible, remove the other 2 from the schema.

b: BreadcrumbList with broken or missing URLs.

items: Breadcrumbs should point to real URLs, not placeholders.
Article schema should have datePublished and dateModified. Missing dates reduce the schema's usefulness.

inline: The fastest full verification is: (1) Rich Results Test on 5 pages (one from each cluster), (2) confirm they show valid and no errors, (3) spot-check the schema on the same 5 pages against visible content, (4) fix anything found. This takes 30–45 minutes and covers the most likely problem cases without validating all 28 pages individually.
The sitemap tells Google which pages exist and when they were last updated. A well-maintained sitemap accelerates indexing, especially for a newly launched cluster.

inline: For pages that remain "Discovered — currently not indexed" for more than 2 weeks, the cause is almost always one of: (1) insufficient internal linking (check the audit), (2) thin content (reconsider the page), or (3) crawl budget issues (larger sites). The fix is usually more internal links and stronger content, not more submissions. Submitting the same URL multiple times does not accelerate indexing.
Search Console is the primary tool for monitoring indexing, search performance, and technical issues. Verify the setup is complete before launching.

inline: In the first 7 days after launch, the analytics to watch are: total sessions (baseline traffic level), pages per session (whether internal linking is working), average time on page (whether content is engaging — for a long-form pillar page, expect 3+ minutes), bounce rate (for cluster pages, high bounce may indicate the page is a dead end or did not match search intent), and conversion events (quote requests and brief downloads are leading indicators; expect low counts in the first week, but any conversions are positive signals).

sections.title: When to Refresh the Cluster Again

inline: A content cluster is not a set-and-forget asset. Search algorithms change, market conditions change, and the cluster itself will age. The refresh schedule below keeps the cluster current.

items: Refresh pricing pages and any page with current-year data (dates, numbers, statistics).
Full internal-link audit (repeat Day 29's process).
Full content refresh — read every page and update anything stale. Reassess whether the cluster structure still makes sense.

b: When a major platform change happens

items: (e.g., Shopify changes its pricing, a major plugin is deprecated, a new platform emerges) — refresh the platform comparison page and any pages that reference the change.

b: When a significant industry change happens

items: (e.g., Google's Helpful Content system updates, AI search behavior changes) — refresh the pages that reference the change, or add a new page addressing it.

blocks.text: Signals that the cluster needs a refresh now

items: Traffic to a page has dropped by 20%+ without an obvious cause.
A page that used to rank on page 1 is now on page 3.
Search Console shows a manual action or coverage error.
A key competitor published a page on the same topic and is ranking above yours.
A significant industry event happened that the cluster does not address.
The "Last updated" date is more than 6 months old.

inline: A refresh is not a rewrite. If a page is fundamentally wrong or irrelevant, it should be merged with another page or removed. If it is slightly out of date, it should be refreshed with current data. The distinction matters: rewriting a page that already ranks well will likely hurt its ranking, while refreshing data on the same page keeps the ranking and improves the content.

faqs.q: How long after launch does the cluster start ranking?
a: Indexing usually happens within 1–7 days. Ranking on page 1 typically takes 30–90 days for new sites, or 1–4 weeks for established sites with existing authority. The cluster structure accelerates this (compared to publishing the same 28 pages without internal linking), but does not eliminate the time required for Google to evaluate the content.

faqs.q: What if pages are not indexed after 30 days?
a: The most common causes are: insufficient internal linking (check Day 29's audit), thin content (each page should have a clear reason to exist), or crawl budget issues (larger sites). The fix is more internal links and stronger content, not more submissions. Submitting the same URL multiple times does not accelerate indexing.

faqs.q: Should I launch the whole cluster at once, or in batches?
a: For a new cluster, launch at once. The internal-link structure only makes sense when all pages exist. For a larger site adding to an existing cluster, you can add in batches — but the new batch should link to the existing cluster and the existing cluster should link back to the new batch within 1–2 weeks.

faqs.q: Can I launch on a Friday?
a: Not recommended. If something goes wrong, you want support available. Launch on a Tuesday or Wednesday, with the following 48 hours reserved for monitoring and fixes. This is the same principle from the process guide — launch on a Tuesday or Wednesday.

faqs.q: What if a page breaks or has an issue after launch?
a: Fix it immediately. Do not wait for a weekly review. Broken pages, checkout bugs, and error pages should be resolved the same day. For content issues (typos, wrong numbers), fix within 24–48 hours. The urgency is different from feature development — live pages are what customers see.

faqs.q: Should I keep the Last updated date current?
a: Yes. Updating the "Last updated" date when you make meaningful changes is honest and helps with freshness signals. Do not update the date without making changes — Google detects this and it can hurt trust.

faqs.q: How do I know if the cluster is working?
a: The signals: (1) pages index within 1–2 weeks, (2) pages start showing impressions in Search Console within 2–4 weeks, (3) some pages start ranking in the top 20 within 30 days, (4) conversion events increase over 60–90 days. If none of these happen after 90 days, the problem is more likely the content than the structure — see the post-launch section.

faqs.q: What is the most important thing after launch?
a: Watching Search Console for indexing issues and Search Console search queries for ranking patterns. The data from Search Console is what tells you which pages to expand, which to consolidate, and which to refresh. It is the feedback loop that turns the cluster from a static asset into a growing one.

faqs.q: Should I add the cluster pages to the main navigation?
a: The top hubs (pillar, geo hub, portfolio, reviews, glossary) should be in the main navigation or footer for depth-1 access. The individual city pages and peripheral cluster pages can remain at depth 2–3 via the hubs. Adding every page to the navigation creates a crowded menu that hurts UX without meaningfully improving crawl.
